newsitem.title: USA: Fed, BOJ won't intervene in FX mart soon - US experts.
newsitem.headline: Fed, BOJ won't intervene in FX mart soon - US experts.

text.p: U.S. foreign exchange experts said chances were slim to none that the Federal Reserve or Bank of Japan would intervene to stem the dollar's rise despite a 50-month peak against the yen on Monday.

Central banks were unlikely to get involved unless the dollar's ascent quickens, it breaks above the critical 130-yen barrier, or U.S. officials temper their strong-dollar rhetoric, currency traders and analysts said.

"At this point, there's absolutely no chance of intervention. The strong dollar is the best thing that has happened to Japan," said John Praveen, senior international economist at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc.
He spoke shortly after the dollar peaked at 125.81 yen, its highest level since January 1993.

Chris Iggo, international economist at BZW Securities Inc in New York, said last week's release of the BoJ's "tankan" survey of business sentiment showed a soft economy and pessimistic corporate outlook for the near-term.
"The only bright spot really is the export sector and a weaker yen will help exports even more," Iggo said.
"For the BoJ to intervene may be a bit of a policy mistake," he added.

Dealers said any effort by U.S. monetary authorities to rein in the greenback would blatantly contradict the strong-dollar policy oft-stated by Treasury officials and fly in the face of Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's remarks last week before a highly publicized trip to Tokyo.

"It would be very counter-productive for the U.S. to intervene when their current stance is for a strong dollar. That would seem very contradictory to me," said Tom Arnold, chief dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
"Most people don't see any possibility of Federal Reserve intervention," he added.
Rubin urged Japan to guard against a resurgence of its trade surplus but stressed that using currency rates to manipulate trade accounts was not the best method.
"If the U.S. was involved in intervention now, it would go against everything Rubin has said," Iggo said.
The Dow Jones industrials index had gained over 45 points and the 30-year long bond had added nearly half a point by mid-afternoon.

"The only damage the dollar seems to be doing is to the U.S.-Japan trade balance and I think the focus is more on inflation than trade, so I would say the odds are pretty low for concerted intervention," he added.
The dollar jumped on Monday despite news of a rise in Japan's current account surplus for the second month in a row. Before January, the trade surplus had shrunk for 17 months.

Traders said Rubin in effect "took the dollar off the table" when it came to trade negotiations between nations, thus allowing the greenback greater freedom on the upside and, in part, sparking Monday's rally.
U.S. asset markets reacted positively to the dollar's strength as overseas investors rushed to capitalize on the move and bought Treasuries and stocks, dealers said.

"It seems to me with both U.S. stocks and bonds rallying that none of the Group of Seven have a real keen interest in intervening," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd in Chicago.
The February surplus rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) from a year earlier.

Dealers also spoke of past failures of central bank intervention in the face of strong economic disparities between nations and of the current inability of nations to alter fiscal policy to manipulate exchange rates.
"There's not much they can do but talk down the dollar. The prospect of the U.S. lowering rates and Japan raising rates is not on the agenda," Merrill's Praveen said.
